r: SWK 1010 surveys the social work profession: its historical and philosophical roots, the fields it touches (health, mental health, policy, child welfare, corrections), and practice with marginalized and oppressed populations. The applied work here is expository, summarizing frameworks, roles, and populations, which task-exposure research classifies among the more automatable knowledge-transmission activities, since explanation and synthesis of established content sits closer to writing than to embodied practice. Still, the course functions as the discipline's gateway survey, and it carries a GT-Pathways Social and Behavioral Sciences designation that mandates its place in the statewide transfer core. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact: AI can summarize social welfare history competently, but institutional lock-in through the GT designation, not task difficulty, is what currently keeps this course required for transfer and program entry into the major.

By 2031, AI will fluently explain social welfare history, professional roles, and policy frameworks on demand, and observed-usage data already shows explanatory and writing tasks as a dominant share of everyday AI use, pushing the realized automatability of this course's expository content upward. The GT-Pathways mandate does not relax on a five-year catalog cycle, so the course remains fixed in the transfer core regardless of how automatable its content becomes. But nothing about the course's structure caps erosion the way a licensure clinical hour or foundational-prerequisite role would elsewhere in the curriculum, so the rating moves to Medium: the survey content itself is increasingly AI-deliverable, even though the transfer requirement keeps the course institutionally necessary. The instrumental case shifts from teaching unique content toward satisfying a fixed general-education slot in the transfer core.

A decade out, AI is a highly capable explainer of social work history, professional roles, and welfare-system structure, and the course's descriptive content is substantially within reach of automation in the central case. The uncertainty is genuine: how gtPathways core requirements evolve, and whether an introductory survey course is reorganized or consolidated, are open questions over a ten-year horizon. But absent a change to the statutory 31-credit general-education transfer core, the GT-SS3 designation continues to require a course of this kind, capping the rating at Medium rather than letting it rise to High. The instrumental case for SWK 1010 rests less on irreplaceable content and more on its fixed role in the transfer curriculum, a constraint that could loosen only through statewide policy change this rating does not assume will happen.
SWK 1010.d: You will be introduced to the profession of social work. You will learn about the historical and philosophical perspectives of generalist social work practice and social welfare programs in response to human needs, human rights, and societal/social problems. You will gain an overview of the social worker's role in the fields of health, mental health, policy, family and child welfare, corrections, and social justice work with marginalized and oppressed populations such as older adults, ethnically and culturally diverse individuals and communities, individuals with disabilities, children, LGBTQIA+ individuals and communities, and other historically oppressed/marginalized individuals, groups, and communities.

r: SWK 1050 surveys human-rights and social-justice frameworks applied to environmental and food justice, healthcare, children's rights, racial justice, immigration, gender, LGBTQ+ rights, criminal justice, and poverty, and teaches theories and methods of political and social change such as advocacy and civic engagement. The graded competence is critical analysis and argument, proposing solutions to complex social challenges, which task-exposure research places among the less-exposed, critical-thinking-intensive activities even as AI drafts fluent policy summaries. The course carries a GT-Pathways Social and Behavioral Sciences designation, mandating its place in the transfer core. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact: AI can generate background on any of these topics, but the course's purpose is training students to analyze and pose solutions themselves, precisely the reasoning work that current evidence treats as resistant to substitution by a model.

By 2031, AI will produce sophisticated policy analysis and advocacy strategy across every topic this course covers, sharpening pressure on the informational half of the course while leaving the critical-reasoning and civic-engagement competence more intact; jagged-frontier evidence suggests students who cannot evaluate AI-generated policy claims risk being misled by confident but wrong analysis. The GT-Pathways mandate holds the course fixed in the transfer core across a catalog cycle regardless of how the content is delivered. Because the underlying tasks (background research, summarization) are meaningfully exposed even as the reasoning core resists, the rating rises to Medium: the instrumental case shifts toward teaching students to interrogate AI-generated social-change analysis rather than to generate it from scratch, while the gen-ed requirement keeps the course institutionally anchored in the curriculum.

Over a decade, AI will be a fluent participant in debates over social and political change, and much of the descriptive and even strategic content this course surveys will be readily AI-generated. The genuinely uncertain question is how gtPathways general-education requirements and course offerings evolve that far out, and whether a course like this persists in its current form. In the central case, the GT-SS3 designation continues to require a Social and Behavioral Sciences transfer course, capping the rating at Medium rather than High, while critical-thinking and civic-reasoning skills remain in the less-automatable band that task-exposure research consistently identifies. The instrumental case rests on the combination of a durable transfer mandate and a reasoning competence that resists full substitution, not on the course's descriptive content alone surviving unautomated.
SWK 1050.d: Operating from human rights and social justice frameworks, this course is an introduction to how to address some of our most pressing social problems. A range of topics will be covered such as environmental and food justice, healthcare, children's rights, racial justice, immigration, gender, LGBTQ+ rights, criminal justice, poverty, and income inequality. The class will include social science content on theories and methods of social and political change such as political advocacy, activism, research, social movements, and civic engagement. Students will hone their critical thinking skills by studying and posing solutions to our nation's complex social challenges.

r: SWK 1600 requires at least 30 hours of direct service at a community organization, paired with reflection on socioeconomic and political factors and a final project connecting the service-learning experience to social problems. The applied work is in-person civic engagement, functioning within an agency, engaging community members, and reflecting on lived context, which sits squarely in the embodied, low-exposure categories that task-exposure research associates with manual and interpersonal work rather than the writing and coding tasks AI performs best. The course also carries a GT-Pathways Social and Behavioral Sciences designation, adding a transfer mandate on top of the embodiment protection. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact: AI can help draft the reflective final project, but it cannot perform the 30 hours of situated community service that is the course's actual requirement.

By 2031, AI tools will assist with logistics, reflection drafting, and analysis of the social problems students encounter at their service sites, but the defining requirement, physically showing up and contributing 30 hours of service within a community organization, is not a task AI can perform on the student's behalf. This in-person, presence-dependent structure keeps the course anchored in the embodied, low-exposure band even as surrounding academic tasks become more AI-assisted, and the GT-Pathways designation keeps it fixed in the transfer core across a catalog cycle. The rating stays Low: unlike coursework built primarily on writing or analysis, this course's core requirement is a physical civic act that written-task automation does not substitute for, regardless of how capable AI writing and research tools become by then.

A decade out, AI may substantially automate the reflective and analytical work surrounding the service experience, but the requirement of direct, situated engagement with a community organization is structurally resistant to automation in the way manual and interpersonal work generally is in the task-exposure evidence. The honest uncertainty is whether service-learning pedagogy itself evolves toward hybrid or virtual civic-engagement models over a ten-year horizon, which could erode the embodiment protection somewhat. But in the central case, the GT-Pathways mandate and the physically embodied service requirement both persist through 2036, holding the rating at Low. The course's instrumental necessity rests on a structural feature, presence at a service site, that is far more durable than any of the analytical tasks surrounding it.
SWK 1600.d: In this course, you will focus on providing a community engaged learning and civic engagement experience from a social work perspective. You will provide at least 30 hours of services to a community organization to enhance your academic and civic learning and complete a final project demonstrating your knowledge of social problems related to your service-learning site. Before beginning the community engaged learning experience, course materials will introduce you to the role of student learning within an agency context. In this class, you will also reflect on social justice issues, understand socioeconomic and political factors that affect our communities, and apply your reflection and learning to your personal and professional development.

r: SWK 3010 teaches the generalist intervention model applied to children and youth, covering developmental needs, rights, and the ecological contexts shaping young people's lives across social service settings. The applied competence is practice judgment with a vulnerable population, assessing developmental context and selecting intervention approaches, which is relational and high-stakes rather than purely informational, placing it in the low-exposure categories task-exposure research associates with client-facing human services work. Verification burden is high because misapplied interventions affecting children carry serious, non-obvious error costs, and the course sits within the CSWE-accredited social work curriculum that structures the practice-methods requirement, even though this population-focused course is one of several practice electives available. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact: AI can summarize child-development theory, but it does not perform the practice judgment the course develops in students.

By 2031, AI will more capably support case documentation, resource matching, and even developmental-assessment drafting relevant to work with children and youth, meaningfully augmenting practitioners. But applying the generalist intervention model to an individual child's circumstances remains judgment-laden and ethically weighty, and the verification burden stays high because errors in practice with minors are costly and not always immediately visible, echoing the jagged-frontier finding that AI users outside a domain's reliable zone are miscalibrated about their own accuracy. The course remains part of the accredited social work program's practice-methods requirement, which does not restructure within a catalog cycle. The rating stays Low: capability grows in the surrounding administrative tasks, but the client-facing practice competence at the center of the course is not what is automating away.

Over a decade, AI could plausibly absorb much of the documentation and resource-navigation work surrounding practice with children and youth, shifting the practitioner's role further toward direct relational judgment and oversight of AI-assisted recommendations. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much of that administrative shell automates and how CSWE-accredited programs restructure practice-methods electives that far out. In the central case, though, the embodied, high-verification-burden core of assessing and intervening with vulnerable children remains a human competence, and the practice-methods requirement within the accredited curriculum persists in some form. Rating holds Low; the clearest change over this horizon is that AI increasingly handles the paperwork around practice with children and youth, not the judgment calls that constitute the course's actual instructional purpose for students.
SWK 3010.d: This course examines how social workers may work effectively with children and youth in a variety of social service settings. This course examines the developmental needs and rights of children and youth, and issues that may emerge in young people's ecological contexts. Students will utilize the social work generalist intervention model to examine best practice approaches with this population.

r: SWK 3020 teaches case management as a foundational social work practice: assessment, intervention planning, service implementation, and monitoring across systems, moving a client from intake through termination. Documentation and service-matching are partially exposed to AI, but the core competence is relational and judgment-laden, building rapport, weighing a client's circumstances, and coordinating services across agencies in person, placing it in the low-exposure, high-presence categories task-exposure research associates with client-facing human services. The binding constraint is the CSWE-accredited social work curriculum feeding the licensure pathway; case management is a mandated practice component of that sequence. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact: AI may draft case notes or surface eligible resources, but it does not perform the client-facing practice competence the course exists to build in students.

By 2031, AI tools for intake support, documentation, benefits navigation, and resource matching will be more capable and more common in social service agencies, meaningfully augmenting caseworkers' administrative load. But client welfare and the interpersonal judgment involved in assessment keep a knowledgeable human necessary, the verification burden is high because errors in service coordination harm real people and failure modes are not always obvious, consistent with the jagged-frontier finding that misapplied AI confidence carries real risk outside reliable domains. Accreditation and licensure requirements for demonstrated practice competency do not relax within a single catalog cycle. The instrumental case remains Low: the caseworker's role shifts toward supervising AI-assisted workflows rather than away from requiring the underlying practice knowledge this course builds in every student.

A decade of capability growth will likely absorb much of the administrative burden of case management, documentation, eligibility checks, scheduling, and could shift the caseworker role further toward relational and supervisory judgment. But the embodied, ethically weighty client practice at the center of the course, and the CSWE accreditation and licensure regime that mandates it, remain binding in the central case through 2036; institutional brakes of this kind change far more slowly than model capability does. The genuine uncertainty is how much of the administrative shell automates around a still-human practice core, not whether case management competency remains required. Rating holds Low; if anything, heavier AI mediation raises the premium on caseworkers able to judge when an automated recommendation is simply wrong.
SWK 3020.d: Case management is a foundational practice within the field of social work. Case management is a process involving the assessment, intervention plan, implementation, and monitoring of services in a variety of social service organizations. The process enables social workers to coordinate services for clients across systems addressing multiple needs. This course will take students through the entire case management process from intake through monitoring to termination.

r: SWK 3030 examines social work practice with older adults and their families: the social context of aging, physiological and social changes that accompany it, and the social worker's role in sustaining and enhancing older clients' functioning and well-being through support systems. The applied competence is relational assessment and coordination with an often-vulnerable population, which sits in the low-exposure, high-presence categories associated with client-facing human services rather than the writing and analysis tasks AI performs best. Verification burden is real because misjudging an older client's support needs or capacity has direct welfare consequences. This population-focused practice course is part of the CSWE-accredited program's broader practice-methods requirement, though not the single course a licensing board names by title. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact: AI can explain aging theory, but not the practice judgment the course builds.

By 2031, AI will more capably support benefits navigation, care-coordination logistics, and even routine check-in communication relevant to work with older adults, augmenting practitioners' administrative capacity considerably. But assessing an older client's changing functional needs and coordinating appropriate support systems remains interpersonal and judgment-laden, and the verification burden stays high because miscalibrated assessments affect vulnerable people's safety and independence, the kind of high-stakes, non-obvious-failure work the jagged-frontier evidence flags as resistant to unsupervised AI substitution. The accredited program's practice-methods requirement persists across a catalog cycle even as individual elective offerings could shift somewhat over time. The rating stays Low: administrative tasks around aging practice increasingly automate, but the relational competence with older clients that the course develops does not automate away with them.

Over a decade, AI could plausibly handle much of the resource navigation, scheduling, and even monitoring documentation involved in supporting older clients, pushing the practitioner's role further toward relational judgment and family coordination. The real uncertainty is how the CSWE-accredited curriculum's practice-methods electives are structured that far out, and whether population-specific courses like this one persist in their current form. In the central case, the embodied work of assessing and supporting older adults' well-being remains a human competence with meaningful verification stakes, and some form of aging-focused practice training remains part of the accredited program. Rating holds Low; the clearer trend is AI absorbing administrative overhead around elder-focused practice, not the direct relational work with older clients that anchors this course's instruction.
SWK 3030.d: This course focuses on social work practice with older adults and their families. The course examines the social context of aging, the aging process, accompanying changes, and the impact on older persons and their families. Emphasis is also on the nature of support systems and the social work role in sustaining and enhancing functioning and well-being.

r: SWK 3040 examines social work interventions using creative modalities, art, drama, music, writing, and physical activities, to facilitate change at micro, mezzo, and macro levels, and studies how selected social work issues have been addressed through these approaches. The graded competence blends creative facilitation technique with critical examination of case examples, which is only partially embodied and carries a moderate verification burden since misapplied creative interventions are less immediately safety-critical than clinical case decisions. As an elective within the CSWE-accredited social work curriculum, it contributes to the program's practice-methods credit total without being the singularly mandated practice course. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact: AI can generate examples of creative interventions from the literature, but designing and facilitating them with real client groups is a practiced skill the course builds directly in students.

By 2031, AI creative and generative tools will be considerably more capable at producing artistic and narrative content, and could plausibly suggest or even co-design creative-intervention activities, meaningfully eroding the course's examination-of-examples component. Facilitation itself, running an art, drama, or music-based intervention with a group in real time, remains more resistant, but the moderate verification burden and moderate embodiment here do not hold the rating down the way a licensure clinical mandate would elsewhere. Because this is an elective contributing to, rather than singularly required for, the accredited program's practice-methods total, the institutional cap loosens earlier than in core practice courses. The rating rises to Medium: the descriptive and design components of the course become substantially AI-assistable, even as live facilitation resists full substitution by a model.

A decade out, AI could plausibly generate sophisticated creative-intervention plans and even simulate their likely effects, substantially eroding the course's design and case-study components. The genuine uncertainty is how much of creative-modality facilitation truly requires an in-person human facilitator versus how much becomes AI-assisted planning executed by a practitioner, and how CSWE-accredited programs treat this kind of elective that far out into the future. In the central case, some embodied facilitation skill remains necessary and the course is not singularly protected by a hard accreditation mandate, holding the rating at Medium rather than High. The instrumental case shifts from learning to devise creative interventions toward learning to adapt and deliver AI-suggested interventions in a live group setting with real clients present.
SWK 3040.d: This course will examine social work interventions that utilize creativity and innovation to facilitate change at micro, mezzo, and macro levels. Creative modalities such as art, drama, music, writing, physical activities, and other innovative practices will be examined for their utility in creating social change. This course will examine how selected social work issues have been addressed using creative modalities.

But applying theory to real practice situations carries interpretive judgment with client-welfare stakes, and the course sits inside the CSWE-accredited social work curriculum required for the licensure pathway, admitting only students formally admitted to the major. At 24 months the instrumental need is intact, held by institutional lock-in and the course's foundational role in the practice sequence ahead.

By 2031, AI will competently explain and even help apply behavioral and change theories to practice scenarios, automating much of the knowledge-delivery function this course currently provides through lecture and assigned reading. But the accredited-curriculum mandate continues to require this foundational theory competence within the social work program across a normal catalog cycle, and applying theory to real, ethically weighty practice situations keeps a knowledgeable human necessary given the client-welfare stakes involved throughout. The rating stays Low: capability growth outruns institutional change on this horizon, and the rating tracks the binding constraint rather than the increasingly AI-deliverable content, the course remains required in the licensure pathway even as its theoretical material becomes something AI explains well to anyone who asks.

A decade out, AI delivers and helps apply social work theory at a high level, and the pure knowledge-transmission rationale for the course is substantially eroded across the curriculum. The institutional cap plausibly relaxes at this horizon: accreditors could revise how theoretical competency is delivered and assessed within a CSWE-accredited curriculum over ten years, so the licensure-driven cap loosens from Low to Medium rather than holding firm as it did before. The rating rises to Medium, the applied knowledge tasks are highly automatable and the mandate is no longer certain to preserve the course unchanged, while interpretive, judgment-laden application of theory to individual and social change, and the real possibility some mandate persists, keep the rating from reaching High at this horizon.
SWK 3050.d: Theories are a framework for understanding human behavior and our larger social world. They guide social workers and helping professionals, providing a framework for working with individuals, families, groups, communities, and organizations to support growth and change. In this course you learn to differentiate between social work perspectives, social theory, and practice theory, and examine how they may be used strategically to guide social work practice. In addition, this course emphasizes the crucial importance of diversity, equity, and inclusion in social work practice, recognizing the multifaceted dimensions of the human experience and the imperative of addressing systemic inequalities. Emphasis is placed on cultivating a deep understanding of the reciprocal relationship between theory and practice, preparing students to apply theoretical frameworks effectively in their roles as social work practitioners.

But applying a practice theory to an actual client system carries client-welfare stakes and non-obvious failure modes, misapplied crisis intervention or narrative technique can cause real harm, so the verification burden keeps a trained human central to the applied work, echoing the jagged-frontier caution about misplaced confidence outside a model's reliable zone. The accredited social work curriculum's licensure pathway does not restructure on a five-year cycle, and this course remains foundational scaffolding for the practicum sequence that follows it directly. The rating stays Low: theoretical content becomes more AI-deliverable, but the applied competence and its institutional mandate both hold firm.

A decade out, AI could plausibly generate sophisticated, theory-grounded intervention suggestions for a wide range of client scenarios, substantially eroding the course's theory-explanation function across the curriculum. The institutional cap plausibly loosens at this horizon, as accreditors could revise how applied-practice-theory competency is taught and assessed within a CSWE-accredited program over ten years, and the foundational-scaffolding protection built on SWK 3050 also weakens once its prerequisite content is more freely AI-deliverable to anyone who needs it. The rating rises to Medium: applying theory to client systems retains real verification stakes that keep it from High, but neither the licensure mandate nor the scaffolding role is certain to hold at full strength through 2036 the way each plainly does nearer-term in the program.
SWK 3060.d: This course expands on content from HBSE I, focusing on how practice theories undergird change processes in social work. This course provides an overview of prominent practice theories, such as cognitive behavioral, crisis intervention, narrative and solution focused theories. Students will engage in the application of social and practice theories within social work settings in order to create meaningful change with client systems.

A decade out, AI could plausibly perform most of the environmental-justice research synthesis and organizing-strategy drafting this course teaches, and the genuine uncertainty is how much community organizing itself becomes AI-mediated versus how much still requires a human building relationships and trust within affected communities over time and across settings. Because the course is a specialized elective rather than a named accreditation requirement, it lacks the strong institutional protection that holds core practice courses down; the rating holds at Medium rather than rising to High, since organizing and coalition-building retain a residual relational core AI does not fully replace. SWK 3070.d: This course will examine how the environment relates to issues of social justice and inequality. Students will examine how environmental issues such as pollution, disasters, and waste sites disproportionately affect marginalized communities. This course examines urban, rural, and suburban spaces, as environmental issues shape individual and community well-being in each of these spaces. Issues of community organizing and activism are examined as tools for effecting change on these topics. Students will apply the generalist intervention model to issues of sustainability, and environmental protection and management.

SWK 3090.d: In this course, you will explore how the frames of history, context, meaning, power, and possibility influence our past and current practice. As part of this exploration, you will learn about epistemology, ethics, values, and other philosophical concepts directly impacting how we think about and act in practice. A deep dive into social work ethics and values provides a necessary foundation for your current ethical student conduct and your future social work practice. Finally, you will develop a framework for how we think in social work, both critically and reflectively, with the intention of reducing bias and increasing possibility.

SWK 3100.d: This course will provide students with an overview of the legal framework for the delivery of child welfare services. It will include federal and state mandates relating to child-abuse prevention and treatment, adoption, and Indian Child Welfare. The role and processes of the court system will be discussed.

Because the course's substance is itself about digital tools and mediums rather than in-person embodied practice, F3=4 reflects low embodiment. Verification burden is moderate (F2=3): misjudging a digital-oppression dynamic or telehealth practice error has real but more correctable consequences than a hands-on clinical mistake. As a curriculum elective rather than the accreditation anchor, F4=3 caps the rating at Medium at 24 months, matching the base case given F1=3 and no dampening from F2 or F3.

By 2031, AI-assisted content generation, digital-literacy instruction, and even telehealth workflow support are plausible extensions of tools already concentrated in computer-and-mathematical and office-task usage per the Anthropic Economic Index. Task-exposure research's finding that writing and digitally mediated tasks are strongly positively associated with exposure applies directly to a course whose subject matter, social media, digital advocacy, telehealth platforms, is itself the domain AI tools already operate in. With F2=3 and F3=4 both above the dampening threshold, and F4=3 no longer binding past 24 months, the base case for F1=4 holds: High. The caveat is that actual telehealth service delivery retains a real client-facing component with privacy and trust stakes the course only partly addresses, so full substitution of the underlying professional skill is not implied, only that the course's instructional content is highly exposed.

A decade out, digital-practice tools such as AI-mediated telehealth triage, automated social-media outreach drafting, and digital-literacy tutoring plausibly become common in the field given compute growth trends compounding over ten years, though Census BTOS diffusion data shows firm-level AI adoption still uneven even at present, a caution against assuming rapid uniform uptake. With no F4 or F5 cap binding past the near term, the rating remains High, tracking the course's fundamentally digital, low-embodiment subject matter. The hedge: whether social work programs redesign this course around AI-native digital practice, or whether ethical and oversight concerns about AI-mediated helping keep the human role central despite technical capability, is not resolvable at this horizon; the rating reflects task exposure, not a claim about how practice will actually evolve.
SWK 3520.d: This course prepares students in social work and allied helping professions to harness technology for social good. We are living in a world that requires our understanding and fluency in a digital language and culture to make change at the micro and macro level. This course examines what it means to be a digital citizen and have digital literacy. Students will explore how power and oppression are present in the most far-reaching areas of our digital world, most of which we don't even see. Finally, this course analyzes digital helping best practices and work on these skills (i.e., telehealth, social media, support groups, public health information) to facilitate change.

r: This course examines the science and strategies of practitioner well-being, mindfulness, positive psychology, and vulnerability, applied to the social worker's own self-care across micro, mezzo, and macro levels. The content is substantially knowledge-and-strategy delivery, mapping to O*NET's updating-and-using-relevant-knowledge and developing-objectives-and-strategies activities, a category observed-usage data shows AI already handling well, since synthesizing wellness literature and generating self-care strategies resembles the writing and knowledge-synthesis work task-exposure research classifies as strongly exposed. Verification burden is low (F2=3): no client is directly at risk from imperfect self-care guidance delivered in an educational context, and F3=4 reflects that the material is largely reflective and digitally deliverable rather than embodied clinical work. As an elective contributing to the accredited curriculum's credit total rather than anchoring it, F4=3 caps the rating at Medium only at 24 months, matching the F1=3 base case.

By 2031, AI-generated mindfulness and positive-psychology content, personalized self-care planning, and wellness-coaching prompts are plausible extensions of tools the Anthropic Economic Index already shows concentrated in writing and knowledge-work usage. This course's substance, synthesizing well-being science and translating it into practitioner strategy, sits squarely in that exposed territory, and productivity research on professional writing shows meaningful quality gains from AI assistance on comparable synthesis-and-drafting tasks. With F2=3 and F3=4 both above the dampening threshold and F4=3 no longer binding past 24 months, the rating tracks the F1=4 base case: High. The caveat is that genuine practitioner self-care and resilience-building may benefit from human mentorship and shared vulnerability in ways an AI-delivered course would not fully replicate, but that is a pedagogical rather than instrumental-need consideration under this rubric.

Ten years out, sustained capability growth per METR/Epoch's task-horizon trend makes it plausible that AI comprehensively delivers well-being science content and generates individualized strategy recommendations at a level matching typical instruction. With no F4 or F5 cap binding past the near term given this course's elective, non-foundational status, the rating remains High. The hedge is calibrated rather than confident: whether social work programs retain a dedicated well-being course taught primarily by faculty, or restructure this content into AI-assisted modules embedded elsewhere in the curriculum, is a design question this rubric does not resolve. What the rating reflects is that the course's actual content, well-being science and strategy synthesis, is squarely within the knowledge-and-writing-adjacent territory that ten years of continued capability growth plausibly renders highly automatable.
SWK 3530.d: Promoting health and well-being are common goals for social work practitioners. This course focuses on healing justice and the role of holistic well-being in professional practice, specifically how practitioners can work on their own holistic well-being while providing care to others. Students will examine the science and strategies of well-being (e.g., mindfulness, positive psychology, vulnerability) while considering all system levels (i.e., micro, mezzo, macro) as possible sources for support and intervention.

r: This course examines social work roles in health and medical settings with special attention to case management: coordinating services, navigating health disparities, and intervening at micro, mezzo, and macro levels around illness and well-being. Case coordination maps to O*NET's assisting-and-caring and coordinating-work-of-others activities, which task-exposure research places among the least automation-exposed categories, since effective case management requires navigating real institutional relationships, patient circumstances, and time-sensitive coordination. Verification burden is high (F2=2): a missed care-coordination step or misjudged disparity-driven barrier carries direct health consequences, and the jagged-frontier research shows AI users are notably less accurate exactly where such situated judgment is needed. As an elective contributing to the accredited curriculum, F4=3 permits a Medium ceiling at 24 months, but the dampened F1=2 base places the actual rating at Low.

By 2031, AI may plausibly assist with health-system documentation, disparities data synthesis, or case-note drafting, tasks reflected in observed office- and writing-usage patterns, but the core work of this course, coordinating actual services for patients navigating illness within an unequal health system, remains embodied, time-sensitive, and interpersonally demanding. Productivity research shows the largest AI gains accrue in structured, lower-stakes tasks like customer support, not in situated healthcare coordination carrying real welfare consequences. With F2=2 and F3=2 both triggering the dampener, the rating stays capped below the F1=3 base case regardless of the F4=3 ceiling, which no longer binds past 24 months. The rating holds Low, reflecting that documentation assistance does not substitute for the judgment-intensive coordination work this course actually teaches.

A decade out, even substantial capability growth in AI-assisted care coordination and disparities analysis does not resolve the core embodiment and verification constraints this course's applied work carries: navigating an actual patient's circumstances within an unequal health system, in real time, with direct welfare stakes if a coordination step is missed. The dampener from F2=2 and F3=2 continues to suppress the rating even as F1 growth would otherwise push toward Medium, and this course's elective status means no institutional cap forces it higher. The rating holds Low, though this carries real uncertainty: healthcare AI adoption is advancing quickly in adjacent areas like documentation and triage support, and if care-coordination tools mature faster than anticipated, the instrumental case for this course's content could shift meaningfully within this horizon.
SWK 3540.d: Promoting health and well-being are common goals for social work practitioners. This course examines issues of health, illness, and well-being within a social and cultural context, particularly in regards to health disparities (e.g., race, class, gender). Students will learn about the myriad roles that social workers play in health and medical settings, with special attention paid to case management. Finally, students will examine strategies to enhance health and well-being through micro, mezzo and macro interventions.

r: This course addresses grief and loss across the lifespan, traditional, ambiguous, and disenfranchised grief, and their implications for social work practice at micro, mezzo, and macro levels. The applied work is direct, emotionally attuned engagement with people experiencing loss, mapping to O*NET's assisting-and-caring and interpersonal-relationship activities that task-exposure research consistently finds low-exposure relative to writing or data tasks. Verification burden is high (F2=2): a mishandled grief intervention risks real psychological harm, and the jagged-frontier finding that AI users are notably less accurate outside well-defined domains is especially salient in emotionally complex, high-stakes therapeutic terrain. As an elective within the accredited curriculum, F4=3 would permit a Medium ceiling at 24 months, but the F2 and F3 dampener pulls the F1=2 base down, and the rating settles at Low.

By 2031, AI may plausibly help draft psychoeducational material on grief stages, generate handouts on ambiguous or disenfranchised loss, or assist with case documentation, reflecting the writing-and-office-task usage the Anthropic Economic Index already shows dominant. But sitting with a grieving client, reading disenfranchised or ambiguous loss that does not fit textbook categories, calibrating real-time emotional attunement, and pacing an intervention to a client's readiness remains squarely embodied, real-time interpersonal work. Productivity RCT evidence shows AI's largest gains concentrate in structured, lower-stakes tasks like customer support, not emotionally complex clinical judgment carrying real psychological stakes. With F2=2 and F3=2 continuing to trigger the dampener and F4=3 no longer providing a floor past 24 months, the rating stays Low, tracking sustained embodiment and verification constraints rather than any institutional lock at this horizon.

Ten years out, even substantial AI capability growth in generating grief-support content or drafting intervention plans does not resolve the fundamental character of this course's applied work: attuned, real-time presence with a person experiencing loss, where misjudged timing or tone causes real harm. The F2/F3 dampener continues to suppress the rating below what F1 growth alone would suggest, and this elective's F4=3 status, contributing to but not anchoring the accredited curriculum, provides no institutional floor at this horizon. The rating holds Low, though with real uncertainty: voice- and affect-aware AI systems could mature in ways that shift the verification calculus for grief-adjacent support tools within a decade, and this analysis does not treat that path as foreclosed, only as insufficiently evidenced by current diffusion and capability data to raise the rating now.
SWK 3550.d: This course will address grief and loss across the lifespan from a social work perspective including traditional, ambiguous, and disenfranchised grief. Students will be provided with information about why and how humans grieve and how grieving is affected by an intersection of characteristics of the person grieving and societal norms. Various types of loss will be discussed alongside implications for social work practice at micro, mezzo, and macro levels.

r: This course supports a teaching-assistant experience with content on pedagogy theory, lesson planning, assessment of student learning, teaching technologies, and classroom and institutional policy, alongside live teaching delivery. Lesson planning and assessment design map to O*NET's training-and-teaching and documenting-information activities, categories task-exposure research finds meaningfully exposed given their overlap with structured writing and content-generation work; observed-usage data confirms office and educational-content tasks are common AI use cases. Live public speaking and in-person classroom facilitation remain embodied, keeping F3 at a moderate rather than low value. Verification burden is moderate (F2=3): pedagogical missteps in a supervised TA role are correctable and lower-stakes than clinical error. This is a supplemental elective requiring program-director approval rather than a core accreditation-anchored requirement, so F4=4 imposes no institutional cap, and the rating tracks the F1=3 base case: Medium.

By 2031, AI-assisted lesson planning, rubric generation, and assessment design are plausible extensions of tools already concentrated in writing and office-task usage per the Anthropic Economic Index, and this course's administrative and content-development components sit squarely in that exposed territory. With F2=3 and F3=3 both above the dampening threshold and no F4 or F5 cap in force, the rating tracks the F1=4 base case: High. The caveat is that the course also builds actual public-speaking and classroom-management competence through supervised live teaching, a real-time, presence-dependent skill AI substitution does not touch, but the instrumental analysis concerns the automatability of the course's applied knowledge tasks overall, and the administrative-and-planning majority of the content, ethical and legal considerations, pedagogy theory, and lesson planning, is highly exposed by this horizon.

A decade out, compounding capability growth documented by METR/Epoch makes it plausible AI comprehensively handles lesson design, assessment construction, and pedagogical-theory synthesis, the bulk of this course's content beyond the supervised teaching placement itself. With F4=4 and F5=4 imposing no institutional or foundational cap, the rating remains High. The hedge: whether BSSW programs retain this elective, approval-gated TA-mentorship structure at all, and whether the live-teaching component itself becomes AI-co-facilitated rather than eliminated, are open design questions this rubric does not resolve. What is defensible is that the specific administrative and content-generation tasks described in this course's catalog text are, by a ten-year horizon, plausibly within AI's demonstrated competence, even as live classroom facilitation and public speaking persist as a human role.
SWK 3560.d: Teaching, public speaking, group dynamics, and program development are key components of social work practice. To cultivate students' skills in these areas, students may apply to work with a faculty mentor as a teaching assistant in supporting the teaching activities. This course supplements and supports the activities that students will perform with support from their faculty mentor. This course examines topics related to teaching in social work, such as ethical and legal considerations, theories of pedagogy, classroom and institutional policies, teaching technologies, assessment of student learning, lesson planning, and classroom dynamics.

r: This course surveys social, historical, legal, and cultural factors shaping immigrant and refugee experience, then applies micro, mezzo, and macro interventions around health, mental health, legal, and family issues for these populations. The historical-legal survey work maps to O*NET's getting-information and interpreting-information-for-others activities, moderately exposed per task-exposure research, while the direct-intervention component maps to assisting-and-caring activities that remain low-exposure. Verification burden is high (F2=2): legal and mental-health stakes for a vulnerable, often precarious population mean an AI error is not a low-cost mistake, and the jagged-frontier finding of reduced accuracy outside well-defined domains applies directly to immigration-status-sensitive advising. As a curriculum elective, F4=3 permits a Medium ceiling at 24 months, but the F2 dampener pulls the F1=2 base down, settling the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI may plausibly synthesize immigration-law background, historical context, and policy analysis competently; task-exposure research finds this kind of structured legal-and-historical synthesis meaningfully exposed, matching the writing- and research-adjacent categories where usage is already concentrated. But applying that knowledge to an actual refugee or immigrant client's precarious legal and family circumstances, health access barriers, or mental-health needs carries real error costs a general-purpose model is not verified to bear reliably. Productivity research's finding that AI's largest uplift concentrates in lower-stakes, well-defined tasks argues against assuming full substitution here. With F2=2 continuing to trigger the dampener and F4=3 no longer providing a floor past 24 months, the rating holds Low, reflecting that the course's protective, high-stakes intervention component outweighs its more exposed knowledge-survey component at this horizon.

A decade out, sustained capability growth plausibly extends AI competence further into legal-context synthesis and intervention-planning support for this population, and the course's F1=4 base case reflects that trajectory. The rating rises to Medium, since F4=3 no longer binds past 24 months and no F5 cap applies, but the dampener's effect on the underlying base, driven by F2=2, keeps the ceiling below High: real-time advising a person facing possible deportation, family separation, or acute mental-health crisis remains high-stakes, judgment-intensive work. This is a meaningful hedge: legal and policy conditions for immigrants and refugees, along with AI's demonstrated reliability in this kind of high-stakes advising, are both genuinely uncertain over a ten-year horizon, and this rating should not be read as a confident prediction of substitution.
SWK 3570.d: In this course students examine the experiences of immigrants and refugees from a social work perspective. This course provides an overview of social, historical, legal, cultural and other environmental factors that shape contemporary experiences of immigrants and refugees within the United States. The course will focus on issues pertinent to these communities, including health, mental health, legal issues, family issues, and intersectional issues of race, class, gender, sexual orientation, ability status, and age. Students will examine micro, mezzo, and macro interventions for supporting immigrants and refugees in the United States.

r: This elective course teaches the social and historical context of military service alongside micro, mezzo, and macro interventions for service members, veterans, and families facing mental health, substance abuse, and violence. AI already drafts psychoeducational material on military culture, VA systems, and common intervention frameworks competently, exposing part of the course's informational content. But applying interventions to a family in crisis carries a high error cost: misjudging suicide risk or intimate-partner violence leaves no safe margin for oversight failure, so verification burden stays low. Task-exposure research finds science and critical-thinking-heavy work resists substitution even where adjacent informational content is exposed. As an elective rather than a licensure-gated core course, institutional lock-in is weaker here than in the required practice sequence, but at this horizon judgment-under-stakes alone keeps the instrumental need intact.

By 2031, AI tools will likely handle much of the descriptive content this course covers — summarizing military culture, benefits systems, and intervention models — and diffusion among human-services agencies will have grown from today's roughly 18 percent of firms using AI. Observed-usage data already shows AI concentrated in office and writing tasks, which overlaps with case documentation here. Yet the course's core purpose is preparing students to weigh intersecting factors — race, gender, disability, age — in real family crises, where the jagged frontier means AI users outside their expertise are measurably less accurate despite feeling confident. Because this is an elective specialization rather than a CSWE-mandated sequence course, institutional protection is thinner, letting the rating rise as informational delivery becomes AI-native even as judgment-in-crisis work resists it.

A decade out, capability trends such as METR's task-horizon doubling suggest AI systems will handle substantially longer, more autonomous intervention-planning tasks, and macro-level diffusion, even if still gradual per Acemoglu's modest ten-year TFP estimates, will have normalized AI-assisted practice planning for military-connected populations. The course's elective status means no accreditation clock protects it the way a licensure-gated practicum would, so its rating is not capped as tightly as required clinical coursework. Still, the interpersonal, high-stakes nature of crisis intervention with veterans and families — trauma, violence, and suicide risk — keeps a real verification floor in place. The central-case forecast is that most of the course's informational scaffolding becomes AI-deliverable while judgment-in-crisis instruction remains necessary, an inherently uncertain ten-year projection.
SWK 3580.d: Members of the military, veterans, and their families face unique challenges in contemporary U.S. society. This course examines the social and historical contexts of military service in the U.S., with particular focus on the issues germane to service members and their families, including issues such as health, mental health, substance abuse, violence, and intersectional issues of race, class, gender, sexual orientation, ability status, and age. A substantial focus of this course involves examining micro, mezzo, and macro interventions for improving the well-being of military members and their families.

r: This course centers Black experiences in social work history, theory, and practice — Afrocentric frameworks, Black social-work leaders, and Black-led social justice movements — and examines how race shapes both practitioners' and clients' experiences in practice settings. The work is discussion- and analysis-heavy rather than clinical-skills training, which is a mixed exposure profile: task-exposure research finds writing tasks positively associated with AI exposure but critical-thinking and culturally-situated interpretive work negatively associated. AI can summarize historical facts and named theorists competently, but centering lived Black experience in practice requires interpretive judgment AI does not reliably replicate. There is no clinical or licensure-clock constraint here — this is an elective, not a required practicum — so the binding constraint at 24 months is the course's critical-thinking core resisting substitution, not institutional lock-in.

By 2031, AI will likely handle more of the historical and theoretical synthesis this course involves — drafting overviews of Afrocentric social work theory or civil-rights-era social justice movements — consistent with observed usage skewing toward writing and office tasks. But the course's central pedagogical aim, centering marginalized experience against a discipline that has historically decentered it, sits in the negatively-exposed critical-thinking category identified by task-exposure research, and AI's demonstrated gaps in nuanced cultural interpretation persist under the jagged-frontier finding that users outside a system's competence zone are measurably less accurate. As an elective with no accreditation-credit floor tied to this specific course, institutional protection is minimal, so the rating rises modestly on exposed content while the interpretive core continues to anchor real coursework value.

Ten years out, capability growth compounds — longer AI task horizons under the METR trend and broader workplace diffusion — making competent AI synthesis of Black social-work history and theory more plausible by default. Because the course carries no course-specific accreditation mandate, nothing structurally prevents its content from being substantially reframed as AI-augmented rather than AI-delivered. Still, the course's central task — training practitioners to center a historically marginalized group's lived experience in practice judgment, not merely recite facts about it — is the kind of interpretive, identity-situated work that macro evidence (modest measured productivity gains) suggests changes more slowly than raw capability implies. This is a genuinely uncertain horizon: the informational layer likely erodes further, but the interpretive core's durability is not something this analysis can confidently forecast.
SWK 3590.d: While Black social workers and clients are often included in content on social work theory, practice, or in conversations about diversity, equity, and inclusion, Black experiences are rarely at the center of these conversations. This course centers Black experiences in social work history, theory, and practice. In this course, students will learn more about our disciplinary and social-historical contexts, including prominent Black social work leaders, Afrocentric social work theories, and Black-led social justice movements (e.g., civil rights, Black Lives Matter). The course will examine how race (and Blackness specifically) shapes Black social workers' experiences in practice settings, as well as the experiences of Black clients and communities.

r: This course applies feminist theory to social work practice, examining how gender is produced and reproduced across individual, group, family, policy, and community levels, alongside concepts of oppression and privilege. Like other critical-theory electives in the program, its core task is interpretive analysis rather than applied clinical skill, placing it in the negatively-exposed critical-thinking category that task-exposure research associates with lower substitution risk, even though AI can competently summarize feminist theoretical frameworks and patriarchal-systems literature — a writing- and knowledge-retrieval task positively associated with exposure. There is no field-placement or licensure-clock element requiring this specific course, and the general-studies field is empty, so no institutional mandate constrains it. At 24 months, the binding constraint is simply that gendered analysis applied to real practice situations resists confident, unsupervised AI substitution.

By 2031, AI assistance with feminist-theory literature review and policy-analysis drafting will likely be routine, consistent with observed-usage data showing office and writing tasks as the largest current use category. That raises exposure on the course's descriptive and synthesis components. However, applying a feminist lens to messy, specific practice situations — gauging how oppression and privilege operate in an actual case, group, or community — remains interpretive work of the kind the jagged-frontier research shows AI users misjudge when working outside a model's reliable zone, with mis-calibrated confidence compounding the risk. As an elective without a course-specific accreditation mandate, the rating is not held down by institutional lock-in, so exposure on the informational layer pushes the overall rating up even as interpretive application stays comparatively resistant.

At ten years, sustained capability growth under trends like METR's task-horizon doubling makes it plausible that AI handles substantially more of this course's theoretical synthesis and even some case-based gendered analysis reasonably well. No accreditation clock protects this specific elective, so nothing structurally prevents its content from being reframed around AI-assisted delivery, and macro adoption evidence points to roughly 0.66 percent cumulative TFP gain over a decade, a modest pace that argues against assuming rapid classroom substitution. Still, the course trains judgment about how gender structures power in live practice contexts — inherently interpretive, high-stakes-adjacent work whose substitution trajectory this analysis cannot confidently pin down given the modest, uneven diffusion patterns documented in macro adoption data. The central-case forecast leans toward continued erosion of the informational core with the interpretive application component remaining a genuine open question at this horizon.
SWK 3600.d: This course examines social work practice from a feminist theoretical perspective. It examines issues of equality, social justice, policy and practice within a patriarchal society. This course examines how gender is produced and reproduced in contemporary society, and how gender matters for social work practice. Multiple levels of practice issues are explored, including individual, group, family, policy, and community. Concepts of oppression and privilege are explored as they relate to people's gendered experiences.

r: This course covers foundational substance-use knowledge, models of care, and interventions, woven through with trauma and identity, framed as anti-oppressive, culturally-responsive, and trauma-informed practice. AI already competently explains substance-use models, screening frameworks, and harm-reduction literature, exposing the course's knowledge-delivery layer. But addiction work carries acute error costs — relapse, overdose, and crisis situations — where a wrong call has no safe margin, keeping verification burden low and a knowledgeable human squarely in the loop. GDPval's finding that even top models still fall short of consistent human-expert performance on real deliverables reinforces the caution warranted here. As an elective rather than a CSWE-mandated practicum course, institutional lock-in is weaker than in the required sequence, but at 24 months the client-safety stakes alone hold the instrumental need for the course.

By 2031, AI will likely be a routine study and intervention-planning aid for addiction content — drafting psychoeducation on models of care or summarizing trauma-informed intervention research — consistent with observed usage concentrated in writing and knowledge-retrieval tasks. That raises exposure on the informational core. Real addiction practice, however, involves reading a person in crisis, judging relapse or overdose risk, and adapting culturally-responsive interventions in the moment — work where the jagged-frontier finding (AI users measurably less accurate and overconfident outside a model's reliable zone) argues for continued close human oversight. With no accreditation-credit floor tied to this specific elective, institutional protection is thin, so the rating rises on exposed content while the safety-critical judgment core keeps a ceiling on full substitution.

At ten years, capability trends (METR's doubling task-horizon, faster compute growth) make broader AI competence in addiction assessment and intervention planning plausible, and workplace diffusion, while still gradual per BTOS-style adoption data, will likely have normalized AI-assisted case preparation in human-services settings. This elective carries no licensure-clock protection, so nothing structurally shields its content from being reorganized around AI-assisted delivery. The genuinely open question is whether verification burden for crisis-level addiction judgment eases enough by 2036 to justify treating AI output as adequately self-checking; current evidence on jagged-frontier miscalibration argues against assuming so. The central-case forecast is substantial erosion of the informational layer with the safety-critical judgment component remaining a hedge against full substitution, and macro-level productivity evidence suggesting only modest, gradual economy-wide change over a full decade reinforces the case for hedging rather than committing to a confident point prediction at this horizon.
SWK 3610.d: Throughout history, substances have been used for ceremony and healing. We have lost our connection to communal use and face a massive addiction epidemic. The way through involves anti-oppressive, culturally-responsive, and trauma-informed interventions, which are essential to social work. This course covers foundational information about substances, models of care, interventions, and systemic factors from a social work perspective. The intersection of trauma, identity, and addiction are woven throughout the course. With the appropriate tools, we can face the multilayered challenges of addiction.

r: This introductory elective examines the relationship between race, gender, and poverty, focusing on the 'feminization of poverty' in the United States and the gap between prevailing stereotypes and empirical realities. The content is largely descriptive social-science analysis — summarizing socioeconomic, age-based, and ethnic factors and contrasting them with data — which sits closer to the writing- and knowledge-synthesis tasks that observed-usage data shows AI already handling heavily in office contexts. There is no field-placement or licensure-clock requirement attached, and the general-studies field is empty, so no institutional mandate constrains it. At 24 months, real classroom deployment and instructor-verification norms remain limited, so the course's descriptive core is exposed in principle but not yet substituted in practice, keeping the rating Low for now — a gap between raw model capability and actual adoption that the diffusion evidence in Census business-survey data on firm-level AI use consistently documents across sectors.

By 2031, AI competently drafting literature reviews and statistical summaries on poverty, race, and gender is plausible given how strongly observed usage already skews toward professional-writing tasks, where RCT evidence shows sizable time savings and quality gains. Because this course leans toward descriptive analysis of documented trends rather than interpretive practice judgment with an actual client, the negatively-exposed critical-thinking protection that shields more clinically-oriented courses applies less strongly here. No accreditation mandate caps the rating, and the course is not foundational to any later required sequence in this catalog area. The combination of thin institutional protection and a largely synthesis-oriented task profile pushes the rating to Medium by five years, though verification of any specific student's argument for accuracy and nuance still benefits from instructor review given the course's introductory level and broad enrollment eligibility.

At ten years, sustained capability growth (METR's task-horizon doubling, continued compute scaling) plausibly extends AI competence to fuller sociological synthesis and data-driven argument construction of the kind this course builds. With no institutional lock-in — no GT designation, no licensure tie, no later-course dependency — nothing structurally protects the course from its descriptive core becoming largely AI-deliverable, and the rating rises to High under the central-case forecast. This is nonetheless a ten-year projection built on capability trends rather than observed classroom substitution, and macro-adoption evidence (modest measured productivity effects to date) counsels real hedging: diffusion into general-studies-style analytical courses could lag capability by years even if the technical case for automation is comparatively strong. Because nothing in the course description ties it to clinical practice, licensure, or a later required course, this is one of the more exposed courses in the batch by the ten-year horizon, with the hedge resting on adoption pace rather than any structural protection.
SWK 3660.d: This course introduces the student to the relationship between race, gender and poverty and examines the underlying causes of the "feminization of poverty" in the United States. Social, economic, age-based and ethnic factors are explored in detail. The differences between prevailing stereotypes and current realities are highlighted.

r: This course trains policy analysis and political advocacy across social-welfare domains — child well-being, aging, health care, poverty, immigration, racial and LGBTQ+ justice — as a dimension of generalist practice. Policy analysis and brief-writing are desk-based, writing-heavy tasks that professional-writing RCT evidence shows AI already accelerates substantially, and observed-usage data confirms writing and office work as the dominant current AI-use category. Misreading a policy's provisions carries real but not immediate-safety-level error cost, so verification burden sits at a moderate rather than protective level. The course contributes to the CSWE-mandated policy-practice competency area without being a course-specific licensure or clinical-hours requirement, giving it a strong but not absolute institutional mandate. At 24 months that mandate, more than any capability limit, keeps the course's instrumental role intact.

By 2031, AI drafting of policy briefs, legislative summaries, and advocacy strategy memos will likely be routine professional practice, consistent with the roughly 75–77 percent automation-leaning usage pattern observed in enterprise API traffic for this kind of knowledge work. The applied task — analyzing how a specific policy affects vulnerable populations and building an advocacy case — is squarely in the programming-and-writing-adjacent, positively-exposed category task-exposure research identifies. The program-level policy-practice competency mandate continues to require the subject area, holding a Medium-band cap rather than allowing the rating to climb unchecked, but within that ceiling the underlying work is substantially AI-deliverable, so the rating reaches that cap by five years. Political advocacy strategy and coalition-building with legislators and community stakeholders still benefit from human judgment and relationship credibility that a drafted brief alone does not supply.

At ten years, continued capability growth under METR's task-horizon trend plausibly extends AI competence to fuller policy-advocacy strategy, not merely drafting, while diffusion across advocacy and human-services organizations — still gradual per Census BTOS adoption figures — normalizes AI-assisted policy work. This course focuses on a variety of topical areas of social welfare policy such as: child well-being; aging; healthcare; mental healthcare; poverty and income inequality; immigration; and policies that impact racial justice, gender equality, and LGBTQ+ rights.
